observations: g_run_method at 0x2bf64 saves 96 register bytes and reserves 528 bytes, a 624-byte fixed frame versus baseline 608. At 0x2c014..0x2c030 it reads nreq and subtracts 16-byte-rounded (nreq+2)*8 from sp; x22 holds the argument address and memset at 0x2c040 initializes it. Measured one-parameter methods need 32 additional stack bytes, so this helper uses 48 more bytes than baseline. There is no managed argument-slot allocation. Return restores sp at 0x2cc60/0x2cc64.

g_job_peer_finish at 0x2b2f8 uses 32 saved-register bytes, clears serving-task/request-task/task-context pointers at 0x2b308/0x2b320/0x2b334 before decrementing existing job owners at 0x2b340. Last-owner path frees peer/status text and tail-calls raw fwp_mem_free at 0x2b384.

fwp_task_own_internal at 0x27ef8 reserves 32 bytes. Unscoped task path branches at 0x27f04 to 0x27f64, stores policy 2 at 0x27f68 and returns without metadata lookup or reference-count traffic. Scoped tasks use the shared-count path.

fwp_free_zombie at 0xe0e0 clears stack and scheduler links at 0xe168..0xe180. Unique policy branches at 0xe188 to disposal at 0xe214, bypassing reference-count lookup. Task storage tail-frees at 0xe260; scoped/shared task policy retains counted disposal.

g_handle at 0x2b38c still uses 1520 bytes including saved registers, matching baseline. User dispatch at 0x2c718 and output continuation fwp_apply at 0x2c84c remain unowned; decoded-value and result ownership are separate work.

All instructions in g_handle, g_run_method, g_job_peer_finish, fwp_task_own_internal, fwp_free_zombie, g_reader and g_accept_loop exactly match the reviewed unary-strings binary. The same stack-slot allocation, ownership branches and disposal paths apply.

binary_observations.limits: Static inspection of ordinary native server binaries, without measurement hooks. No downloaded program executed. Inlined helpers may lack standalone symbols; inspect instructions, ownership operations and register/stack use. No timing or zero-overhead claim follows from symbols.

observations: g_run_method 0x2fb00 has a 504-byte fixed frame excluding incoming return address (456-byte reservation plus 48 saved-register bytes), plus 16-byte-rounded argument storage. The measured one-parameter methods need 32 extra stack bytes for three value words, versus baseline 488-byte fixed frame and heap slots. At 0x2fbac it reads nreq; 0x2fbb3..0x2fbc2 rounds size and adjusts rsp; 0x2fbd2 zeroes the slots, whose address is in r13 and spills to rbp-0x98. No allocator call for argument slots. 0x30901 restores rsp from rbp.

g_job_peer_finish 0x2eaf0 clears serving task at 0x2eaf5, request task at 0x2eb0f and task context at 0x2eb2a. The existing owner count decrements at 0x2eb3e; zero frees peer/status text and tail-calls fwp_mem_free at 0x2eb75. One saved rbx word is used.

fwp_task_own_internal 0x2b0d0 branches on scope ownership. No scope takes 0x2b156, stores unique policy 2 and returns, without allocation-metadata access or reference-count traffic. Scoped tasks take the counted path. It saves 24 bytes.

fwp_free_zombie 0xe9e0 clears stack storage at 0xea3b and scheduler links before loading policy at 0xea90. Unique policy branches at 0xea99 past count lookup to disposal, reaching raw fwp_mem_free at 0xeb97. Shared scoped tasks retain their own count path.
g_handle retains its baseline 1496-byte frame; decoded values and unowned g_apply_user invocation remain. No timing or complete GC-removal claim.

All instructions in g_handle, g_run_method, g_job_peer_finish, fwp_task_own_internal, fwp_free_zombie, g_reader and g_accept_loop exactly match the reviewed unary-strings server. The same argument-stack allocation, owner branch and job/task disposal apply.

hosts.scope:
# Measuring memory in a server after repeated calls

A remote call runs part of a program in another process. Earlier client
measurements exclude that server process; they cannot prove its values or
serving tasks are released. This baseline measures the native server itself.

Each client takes a call count on the command line. `I64` is a signed 64-bit
integer. `consume : I64 -> I64` takes a call index and returns its numeric result;
the channel variant adds `! {Async}` to declare task/channel operations.
`const` supplies the same input for each call; `step` adds the response to an accumulated total. `curry`
adapts the tuple-taking body of `step` to the two arguments supplied by fold.
The four workloads are:

- `unary-strings`: send a 64-character name and receive a greeting. The server
  adds the seven characters `hello, `, so each result has length 71.
- `response-stream`: ask for integers 1 through 64 and sum them, giving 2,080.
  An iterator produces these values as the caller requests them.
- `request-stream`: send those 64 integers and receive their sum, 2,080.
- `channel-output`: ask the server to send `tick 1` through `tick 64` into a
  channel, a queue used to communicate between tasks. Close and drain the queue
  after the call, then add the string lengths, giving 439.

Each measured server process receives 1, 16 or 256 sequential calls from one
client, with three fresh server processes per case. The client uses ordinary
connection reuse. Samples follow serving-task removal from the scheduler;
physical task-record freeing is measured separately by the resulting managed
storage. The final sample waits for client disconnection and removal of all
connection and serving tasks. The server remains alive with its listener open.

Generated clients and servers use native `-O2`. Collection is disabled and
physical freeing enabled. Counters begin after
listener, routing and root-task setup. They cover managed allocation requests,
requested/charged bytes, reference-count increments and selected allocation
categories. Categories count allocations, not identities of remaining objects.
Raw request/wire buffers, stack pools, TLS/OS/allocator metadata, whole-process
memory and timing are excluded. Both an interpreted server and ordinary native
server provide functional output references. No timing or C/Rust comparison is
claimed; the baseline does not establish server ownership or checked ARC.

An idle scheduler can remain on the last finished task's stack until another
task becomes ready. The measurement wakes the existing listener once, after
the connection closes and all spawned tasks finish, so the ordinary scheduler
can retire that final task before sampling. This adds no task or connection;
comparisons must use the same wake and drain boundary.
